title: Machine-Learned Compact Subspace Generation for Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction within Density Matrix Embedding Framework
summary: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD), an extension of Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction (QSCI), has emerged as a promising hybrid quantum-classical paradigm for computing molecular ground state energies. By leveraging quantum sampling instead of variational optimization, QSCI avoids barren plateaus and enables direct reconstruction of correlated electronic wavefunctions. However, existing configuration recovery techniques primarily enforce symmetry constraints without guaranteeing optimal selection of the most physically relevant configurations, often leading to unnecessarily large subspaces and increased classical diagonalization costs. In this work, we introduce a machine-learned compact subspace generation protocol based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), termed QSCI-RBM, and integrate it within the Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) framework. The RBM is trained on quantum-sampled configurations to learn the underlying probability distribution of dominant determinants, enabling the targeted generation of high-probability configurations. We apply this framework to the simulation of a protein-ligand complex involving the inhibitor Carmofur bound to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease ($M^{\text{pro}}$). Our results demonstrate that DMET-QSCI-RBM achieves energies within the chemical accuracy threshold by accessing only approximately 4% of the configuration subspace. In contrast, standard DMET-SQD simulations failed to reach chemical accuracy while accessing up to 20% of the subspace, even as the chemical potential itself nearly converged. These findings highlight that RBM-assisted configuration generation produces significantly more compact subspaces while preserving physical accuracy, thereby reducing classical computational overhead and enabling the scalable quantum embedding simulation of complex biological systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces QSCI-RBM, a machine-learned protocol using Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) to generate compact configuration subspaces for quantum diagonalization. Integrated within DMET, it achieves chemical accuracy for a SARS-CoV-2 M^pro protein-ligand complex using only ~4% of the configuration subspace, whereas standard SQD fails to reach chemical accuracy even with 20% of the subspace.
AI.motivation: Existing configuration recovery techniques in SQD/QSCI enforce symmetry constraints without guaranteeing optimal selection of physically relevant configurations, leading to unnecessarily large subspaces and increased classical diagonalization costs.
AI.method: The authors propose QSCI-RBM, which trains a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) on quantum-sampled configurations to learn the probability distribution of dominant determinants, enabling targeted generation of high-probability configurations. This is integrated within the Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) framework.
AI.result: DMET-QSCI-RBM achieves energies within chemical accuracy using only ~4% of the configuration subspace, while standard DMET-SQD fails to reach chemical accuracy even when accessing up to 20% of the subspace.
AI.conclusion: RBM-assisted configuration generation produces significantly more compact subspaces while preserving physical accuracy, reducing classical computational overhead and enabling scalable quantum embedding simulations of complex biological systems.

title: Autonomization of Quantum Systems and the Emergence of the Work Operator
comment: 11 pages main text, 37 pages appendix, 1 figure. Comments welcome :)
summary: Estimation of work at the quantum scale remains a central challenge in quantum thermodynamics. Canonical approaches have a fundamental drawback: they assume classical control of the quantum system, as implicit in a time-dependent Hamiltonian. Yet the energetic cost of implementing this control is omitted and can exceed the system's energy scale by orders of magnitude, calling into question the operational significance of work values. We address this by autonomizing the controlled energy transfer, embedding the driven dynamics into an energy-conserving evolution on a larger quantum system. Work is then unambiguously identified with the energy transferred between the two systems, singling out a unique observable on the driven system: the work operator. We show that the quantum work operator evades a no-go theorem by deriving a quantum fluctuation theorem that recovers the Jarzynski equality in classical scenarios. We incorporate imperfect control and quantify corrections to work statistics. Extending the framework to open quantum systems, we obtain an operatorial first law in which work, heat, and internal-energy changes are represented by distinct operators on the reduced system. Together, these results settle the long-standing debate over whether work is a quantum observable: it is, once the controlling system is included in the description rather than treated as external.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the question of whether work is a quantum observable by embedding driven quantum systems into an energy-conserving larger system, defining a work operator that satisfies a quantum fluctuation theorem and an operatorial first law for open systems.
AI.motivation: Standard approaches to quantum work assume classical control via time-dependent Hamiltonians, but ignore the energetic cost of implementing that control—which can far exceed the system's energy scale—thus questioning the operational meaning of work.
AI.method: The authors autonomize the controlled energy transfer by embedding the driven dynamics into a larger, energy-conserving quantum system, and identify work with the energy transferred between the two systems, yielding a unique work operator.
AI.result: They derive a quantum fluctuation theorem that recovers the Jarzynski equality in classical limits, quantify corrections from imperfect control, and extend the framework to open systems to obtain an operatorial first law with distinct work, heat, and internal-energy operators.
AI.conclusion: Work is a genuine quantum observable once the controlling system is included in the description rather than treated externally, settling a long-standing debate.

title: Perturbatively Stable Self-Correcting Classical Memory from Gauge Averaging
summary: We show that the self-correcting memory in 3d Wegner gauge theory is stable to arbitrary small enough perturbations of the Hamiltonian. Our proof relies on a new method we dub ``gauge averaging'', which gives conditions under which explicitly broken gauge symmetries are effectively restored by fluctuations. These conditions show that the self-correcting memory phase is fluctuation stabilized, with its robustness to perturbations increasing with increasing temperature, up to some $T_c > 0$.

AI.tldr: Self-correcting memory in 3d Wegner gauge theory is stable against small Hamiltonian perturbations, proven by a new "gauge averaging" method showing broken gauge symmetries are restored by fluctuations, with robustness increasing with temperature up to Tc > 0.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the stability of self-correcting quantum memory in 3d Wegner gauge theory under perturbations, addressing whether topological protection survives in realistic, imperfect settings.
AI.method: Introduces "gauge averaging"—a technique that identifies conditions under which explicitly broken gauge symmetries become effectively restored through thermal/quantum fluctuations, proving the memory phase is fluctuation-stabilized.
AI.result: The self-correcting memory phase is stable to arbitrarily small Hamiltonian perturbations; robustness counterintuitively grows with increasing temperature up to a critical temperature Tc > 0.
AI.conclusion: Fluctuations can stabilize topological protection in gauge theories, enabling robust self-correction in 3D without requiring perfect symmetry.

title: Driven criticality links universal computation and optimal representations
summary: Near-critical dynamics are often linked to enhanced computation, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. We address this question in reservoir computing, where a fixed recurrent network maps input sequences into high-dimensional states and only a simple readout is trained. We extend fixed-reservoir universality results to discrete-time input-driven reservoirs and connect their key geometric condition, neighborhood separation, to dynamics. To this end, we introduce a finite-resolution neighborhood separability index and an input-conditioned maximal Lyapunov exponent. We find that neighborhood separability, chaotic time-series prediction, and smooth high-dimensional representation geometry are optimized in the same narrow window of marginal driven stability. In this regime, the covariance spectrum approaches the power-law scaling expected for near-optimal smooth representations. Our results link edge-of-instability computation, universality, readout performance, and optimal representation geometry within a common dynamical framework.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why near-critical dynamics enhance computation in reservoir computing, finding that optimal performance occurs at the edge of instability where neighborhood separability, prediction accuracy, and smooth high-dimensional representations converge, with covariance spectra showing power-law scaling.
AI.motivation: The mechanism by which near-critical dynamics enhance computation remains unclear, and the authors aim to clarify this by studying input-driven discrete-time reservoir computers.
AI.method: The authors extend fixed-reservoir universality results to discrete-time input-driven reservoirs, introduce a finite-resolution neighborhood separability index and an input-conditioned maximal Lyapunov exponent, and analyze the covariance spectrum scaling.
AI.result: Neighborhood separability, chaotic time-series prediction, and smooth high-dimensional representation geometry are all optimized within the same narrow window of marginal driven stability, where the covariance spectrum exhibits power-law scaling.
AI.conclusion: Edge-of-instability computation, universality, readout performance, and optimal representation geometry are linked within a common dynamical framework.

title: Enabling Neutral Atom Integration: Redesigning Device Models for Universal Quantum Ecosystems
summary: Quantum computing is transitioning from an academic idea to a practical technology, driven by recent hardware advancements and clear paths toward real-world applications. Universal quantum ecosystems (e.g., Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane) facilitate this transition by providing a consistent interface to diverse quantum devices, abstracting hardware-specific details through a device model that captures each device's computational capabilities. However, these device models have historically been shaped by superconducting hardware, assuming static qubit positions and fixed coupling maps. This prevents them from representing the unique computational capabilities of emerging technologies such as neutral atoms, which feature dynamic qubit rearrangement and zoned operations. As a result, although numerous specialized compilers for neutral atom devices already exist, they cannot retrieve the hardware information they need through these ecosystems - creating a technology lock that hinders or even prevents the integration of neutral atom devices. In this work, we demonstrate how this limitation leads to suboptimal compilation results and can exclude certain devices entirely. Motivated by this, we propose rethinking current device models to faithfully represent neutral atom devices, enabling their seamless integration into universal quantum ecosystems. Evaluations conducted within the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI) demonstrate that the proposed device model unlocks a routing overhead fidelity improvement by a factor of up to 100,000 on a circuit with 16 qubits and 600 gates.

AI.tldr: Current universal quantum ecosystems use device models designed for superconducting hardware (static qubits, fixed coupling), which cannot represent neutral atom devices' dynamic rearrangement and zoned operations. This creates a technology lock that degrades compilation and excludes these devices. A new device model is proposed, achieving up to 100,000x routing overhead fidelity improvement on a 16-qubit, 600-gate circuit.
AI.motivation: Universal quantum ecosystems (Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane) use device models based on superconducting hardware assumptions (static qubit positions, fixed coupling maps), which fail to represent emerging neutral atom devices with dynamic qubit rearrangement and zoned operations. This creates a technology lock that hinders or prevents their integration.
AI.method: The authors analyze limitations of current device models when applied to neutral atom devices, then propose rethinking device models to faithfully represent neutral atom computational capabilities (dynamic rearrangement, zoned operations). The proposed model is evaluated within the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI) framework.
AI.result: The proposed device model achieves a routing overhead fidelity improvement by a factor of up to 100,000 on a circuit with 16 qubits and 600 gates compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Current device models in universal quantum ecosystems impose a technology lock that disadvantages neutral atom devices. A redesigned device model that faithfully captures neutral atom capabilities enables seamless integration and dramatically improves compilation fidelity.

title: Learning the closest Slater determinant
summary: Learning compact, interpretable descriptions of quantum many-body states is an important task in quantum science. We study the task of learning the Slater determinant with maximum fidelity to an arbitrary fermionic many-body state, with motivation from both Hartree-Fock methods and agnostic tomography. Given an $n$-fermion wavefunction built from $m$ fermionic modes, we provide classical and quantum algorithms returning a Slater determinant with fidelity within $\varepsilon$ of maximal in time $m^{\text{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)}$. We prove matching hardness lower bounds, assuming standard complexity conjectures, along some parameter axes. Given access to quantum copies, we prove this can be accomplished with $\text{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon)$ copies of $ρ$. We also show that above a fidelity of $2/3$ any stationary point is the unique global maximum while below $2/3$ the optimization landscape can have spurious stationary points, and hence $2/3$ marks a transition point in the optimization landscape for this problem. We apply the algorithm to the Fermi-Hubbard model, extracting the closest Slater determinant from neural quantum state solutions. Together, our results provide algorithmic tools with provable guarantees in understanding fermionic many-body systems with classical or quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the problem of finding the Slater determinant with maximum fidelity to an arbitrary fermionic many-body state, providing classical and quantum algorithms with provable guarantees, matching hardness lower bounds, and identifying a fidelity transition point at 2/3 in the optimization landscape.
AI.motivation: Learning compact, interpretable descriptions (Slater determinants) of quantum many-body states is important for both Hartree-Fock methods and agnostic tomography, with applications in understanding fermionic systems.
AI.method: The authors provide classical and quantum algorithms that return a Slater determinant with fidelity within ε of maximal in time m^{poly(n,1/ε)}. They also prove matching hardness lower bounds assuming standard complexity conjectures, and show that with quantum copies the task can be accomplished using poly(m,n,1/ε) copies of ρ. They analyze the optimization landscape, proving a transition at fidelity 2/3.
AI.result: Algorithms with provable runtime guarantees; matching hardness lower bounds; identification of a sharp transition at fidelity 2/3 where above this threshold all stationary points are global maxima while below it spurious stationary points appear; application to Fermi-Hubbard model extracting closest Slater determinants from neural quantum states.
AI.conclusion: The results provide algorithmic tools with provable guarantees for understanding fermionic many-body systems via classical or quantum simulation, with a clear characterization of the optimization landscape.

title: HI-QDC: An Isometric Modular Scalable Architecture for Quantum Data Centers
summary: Server-centric quantum data-center architectures offer scalability by distributing communication tasks across QPUs rather than concentrating complexity in a centralized switching core. However, scaling such architectures increases the path length, the number of Bell-state measurements, and the loss of end-to-end fidelity. We ask whether the path diversity of a server-centric topology can be converted into a mechanism for preserving not only rate, but also fidelity. We study this through end-to-end purification as a fidelity-restoration mechanism. First, in a black-box model, we determine the minimum number of raw end-to-end Werner-state copies, each carrying the degraded Werner parameter of a distance-ell path, that purification must consume to recover a single copy matching an elementary link, comparing recursive 2-to-1 and optimized nested r-to-1 purification. Second, we instantiate these requirements in a probabilistic BCube architecture, whose edge-disjoint path diversity supplies the raw copies. Because purification imposes a lower bound on input fidelity, no path redundancy can raise the output below this threshold, which limits scaling. To address it we present the Hop-Independent Quantum Data Center (HI-QDC), an isometric, modular, scalable architecture in which purification transforms end-to-end entanglement across a module into an effective link-level resource for the inter-module topology. Our results identify the regimes in which a BCube module, under end-to-end purification, preserves both the fidelity and the yield of an elementary link. The module then hides its internal hop count and acts as an effective elementary link for a higher-level network. Thus topology supplies the path multiplicity purification requires, while purification converts it into fidelity recovery, enabling recursively scalable quantum data-center networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using path diversity in server-centric quantum data centers for end-to-end fidelity restoration via purification, introduces HI-QDC architecture that hides internal hop count, and shows conditions where a BCube module preserves fidelity like an elementary link for recursive scaling.
AI.motivation: Server-centric quantum data centers scale by distributing communication tasks across QPUs, but increasing path length, Bell-state measurements, and loss of end-to-end fidelity hinder scaling. The authors ask whether path diversity can preserve not only rate but also fidelity.
AI.method: Analyzes minimum raw Werner-state copies needed for purification to match elementary link fidelity (recursive 2-to-1 vs. optimized nested r-to-1). Instantiates in probabilistic BCube architecture using edge-disjoint path diversity. Proposes HI-QDC: an isometric, modular, scalable architecture where purification transforms end-to-end entanglement into effective link-level resource for inter-module topology.
AI.result: Shows purification imposes a lower bound on input fidelity; no path redundancy can raise output below threshold, limiting scaling. Identifies regimes where a BCube module under end-to-end purification preserves both fidelity and yield of an elementary link.
AI.conclusion: Topology supplies path multiplicity for purification; purification converts it into fidelity recovery. The module hides internal hop count and acts as an effective elementary link, enabling recursively scalable quantum data-center networks.

title: Unitary $k$-designs without Hamiltonian quenches
summary: Unitary designs provide an efficient means of emulating Haar randomness without the requirement of exponential resources. Hamiltonian quench protocols have recently been shown to generate such designs, but achieving this typically requires multiple independent Hamiltonian quenches, even via temporal ensembles. Here, we show that no Hamiltonian quenches are required: a single chaotic Hamiltonian is sufficient to generate approximate unitary $k$-designs. We introduce a two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol, where unitary evolution under a fixed Hamiltonian is interspersed with two Pauli operator insertions (kicks). By evaluating the frame potential, we demonstrate that the resulting ensemble converges to the Haar value, indicating the emergence of approximate unitary designs. We verify this protocol for Gaussian random matrix ensembles, the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, and simplified spin (bosonic) SYK models. Furthermore, our protocol admits a canonical definition of finite-temperature frame potentials and establishes the relation with the partition function. We outline a plausible holographic interpretation of our protocol from the dual gravity picture.

AI.tldr: A single chaotic Hamiltonian with just two Pauli kicks can generate approximate unitary k-designs, eliminating the need for multiple independent Hamiltonian quenches. Verified across Gaussian ensembles, SYK models, and spin SYK models, the protocol also yields finite-temperature frame potentials and a holographic interpretation.
AI.motivation: Unitary designs emulate Haar randomness but typically require multiple independent Hamiltonian quenches, even in temporal ensembles. The goal is to achieve this with minimal resources—specifically, using a single fixed chaotic Hamiltonian without any quenches.
AI.method: A 2PK protocol: unitary evolution under a fixed chaotic Hamiltonian is interspersed with two Pauli operator insertions (kicks). The ensemble's convergence to Haar randomness is assessed via the frame potential. Tested on Gaussian random matrices, the SYK model, and spin (bosonic) SYK models. A finite-temperature frame potential is canonically defined and linked to the partition function.
AI.result: The 2PK ensemble's frame potential converges to the Haar value, confirming approximate unitary k-designs. The protocol works across all tested models. A finite-temperature frame potential is defined, and a connection to the partition function is established. A holographic dual gravity interpretation is outlined.
AI.conclusion: A single chaotic Hamiltonian with two Pauli kicks suffices to generate approximate unitary designs, significantly reducing resource requirements. The protocol bridges quantum chaos, random matrix theory, and holography, offering a practical path to Haar-random emulation.

title: Detecting Hidden Nonlinear High Frequency Modes Beyond Fundamental Minimal Temporal Resolution Using Weak Measurements
summary: In this work we study whether nonlinear models of quantum mechanics can avoid detection by strong measurements, if the nonlinear effects only exist as high frequency modes. A potential physical process which could hide such modes would be amplitude level time averaging over fundamentally indistinguishable times. To that end, we have defined a temporal indistinguishability postulate which describes the averaging process, and handcrafted a nonlinear toy model well suited to avoid detection. We have demonstrated that even in such an ideal setup, tabletop weak postselected measurements can still detect nonlinear behavior and put constraints on nonlinear high frequency modes of evolution, even at frequencies beyond fundamental minimal temporal resolution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether nonlinear quantum mechanical effects existing only at high frequencies can evade detection through strong measurements, and demonstrates that weak postselected measurements can still detect such nonlinear behavior and constrain high-frequency modes beyond fundamental temporal resolution limits.
AI.motivation: To determine whether nonlinear quantum mechanical effects that only manifest at high frequencies can remain undetected under strong measurements, potentially hiding them from experimental observation.
AI.method: The authors define a temporal indistinguishability postulate describing amplitude-level time averaging over fundamentally indistinguishable times, and construct a handcrafted nonlinear toy model designed to avoid detection by strong measurements.
AI.result: Even in this ideal setup designed to evade detection, tabletop weak postselected measurements can still detect nonlinear behavior and impose constraints on nonlinear high-frequency modes of evolution, even at frequencies beyond the fundamental minimal temporal resolution.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear quantum effects cannot easily evade detection through high-frequency hiding; weak postselected measurements provide a powerful tool for constraining such effects at frequencies beyond the minimal temporal resolution.

title: Finite Key Underwater Quantum Key Distribution: Performance Analysis and Improvements
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) allows for the establishment of a secret key between two parties, secure against computationally unbounded adversaries. Most experimental and theoretical research in this area, investigates the performance of QKD over fiber or free space channels. A growing body of work, however, has begun to investigate its performance in underwater scenarios. Here, we consider the realistic finite key scenario, and evaluate the simulated performance of two different decoy state protocols. We show that there are certain underwater channels where "simpler" QKD protocols outperform more complex ones. Finally, we also investigate methods to improve QKD performance underwater, specifically looking at classical advantage distillation, which we show can greatly improve the maximal distance supported by QKD underwater.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the performance of quantum key distribution (QKD) in underwater scenarios under realistic finite key conditions, comparing two decoy state protocols and showing that simpler protocols can outperform complex ones in certain underwater channels, while also demonstrating that classical advantage distillation significantly improves the maximal distance supported by underwater QKD.
AI.motivation: While QKD has been extensively studied over fiber and free-space channels, its performance in underwater scenarios is less understood. This work aims to fill that gap by evaluating realistic finite-key performance of QKD protocols underwater.
AI.method: The authors simulate two different decoy state QKD protocols in underwater channels under realistic finite key scenarios. They also investigate classical advantage distillation as a method to improve performance.
AI.result: Simpler QKD protocols can outperform more complex ones in certain underwater channels. Classical advantage distillation greatly improves the maximal distance supported by underwater QKD.
AI.conclusion: Underwater QKD performance depends on channel conditions, and simpler protocols may be preferable in some cases. Classical advantage distillation is an effective technique for extending the operational range of underwater QKD.

title: Bistability of Exciton-Photon Microcavities in the Ultrastrong-Coupling Regime
summary: We investigate a coherently driven exciton--photon microcavity with Kerr nonlinearity in the ultrastrong-coupling regime. When the lower and upper polariton branches are well separated in energy, the full Hopfield--Rabi--Kerr model reduces to an effective single-mode description of the lower polariton. We analyze the stability of the lower-polariton steady states. We show that the resulting bistability is qualitatively similar to that in the strong-coupling regime. However, in the ultrastrong-coupling regime counter-rotating processes and the diamagnetic $A^{2}$ term renormalize the polariton spectrum and composition, changing the effective detuning $\tildeΔ_{1}$ and nonlinearity $U_{\mathrm{LP}}$ $g$-dependency beyond the strong-coupling (RWA) picture. As a result, although the semiclassical bistability criterion keeps its standard Kerr--oscillator form, the turning points and hysteresis window are shifted relative to the strong-coupling prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how a coherently driven exciton-photon microcavity with Kerr nonlinearity behaves in the ultrastrong-coupling regime. The system reduces to an effective single-mode lower polariton model, and while bistability qualitatively resembles the strong-coupling case, counter-rotating processes and the diamagnetic A² term renormalize the polariton spectrum, effective detuning, and nonlinearity, shifting the bistability turning points and hysteresis window relative to strong-coupling predictions.
AI.motivation: To understand how the ultrastrong-coupling regime modifies the nonlinear dynamics and bistability of driven exciton-photon microcavities, which cannot be captured by the standard rotating-wave approximation (RWA) used in strong-coupling theory.
AI.method: The authors derive an effective single-mode description of the lower polariton from the full Hopfield–Rabi–Kerr model when polariton branches are well separated. They perform a stability analysis of the lower-polariton steady states and derive a semiclassical bistability criterion.
AI.result: Bistability in the ultrastrong-coupling regime is qualitatively similar to strong coupling, but counter-rotating and diamagnetic A² terms renormalize the effective detuning Δ̃₁ and nonlinearity U_LP, altering their g-dependency. The turning points and hysteresis window are shifted compared to strong-coupling (RWA) predictions, though the semiclassical bistability criterion retains the standard Kerr-oscillator form.
AI.conclusion: Ultrastrong coupling introduces quantitative corrections to polariton bistability via renormalized parameters, even though the qualitative bistability behavior and the formal structure of the bistability criterion remain unchanged from the strong-coupling regime.

title: Fermionic Genuine Multiparty Entanglement
summary: Entanglement can show fundamentally different behavior in fermionic systems. However, while bipartite measures of fermionic entanglement have been established, genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) in fermionic systems is much less understood. We introduce an efficiently computable measure (via semi-definite programming) of fermionic GME, fermion genuine multiparty negativity (fGMN), and show that it is an entanglement monotone and a natural multipartite extension of the fermionic negativity. Using this measure, we find many states which have fGMN but no non-fermionic GME, including large classes of fermionic stabilizer states. The fGMN also displays some major phenomenological differences to the bipartite fermionic negativity, such as finite sudden death points over separation and temperature.

AI.tldr: Introduces fermion genuine multiparty negativity (fGMN), a computable measure of genuine multiparty entanglement in fermionic systems, showing it captures entanglement undetected by non-fermionic measures and exhibits distinct phenomena like finite sudden death.
AI.motivation: While bipartite fermionic entanglement measures exist, genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) in fermionic systems is poorly understood; this work aims to provide a computable and monotonic measure for fermionic GME.
AI.method: Defines fGMN via semi-definite programming, proving it is an entanglement monotone and a multipartite extension of the fermionic negativity; analyzes its behavior on fermionic stabilizer states and across separation/temperature variations.
AI.result: Many states (including large classes of fermionic stabilizer states) have fGMN but no non-fermionic GME; fGMN shows finite sudden death points over separation and temperature, unlike bipartite fermionic negativity.
AI.conclusion: fGMN is a valid, efficiently computable GME measure for fermionic systems, revealing fundamentally different multiparty entanglement behavior compared to both non-fermionic and bipartite fermionic measures.

title: Suppressing errors in analog logical rotation gates via balanced fusion
summary: There have been a number of recent proposals to use analog logical rotations in early fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. Existing proposals implement a logical rotation by angle $φ$, with error $O(pφ)$, where $p$ is the physical error rate. While this is not fault-tolerant, if $φ$ is sufficiently small the logical error rate can be suppressed. In this work, we introduce and analyze the `balanced fusion' technique for improving the error scaling of analog logical rotations to $O(p φ^{1.5})$, without having to resort to fallback synthesis. Balanced fusion is enabled by an improved analysis of the accumulation of coherent error terms in analog logical rotations. Our techniques improve the viability of analog logical rotations for small rotation angles as an alternative to cultivation-powered rotation synthesis.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "balanced fusion" to improve error scaling of analog logical rotations from O(pφ) to O(p φ^{1.5}) without fallback synthesis, via better analysis of coherent error accumulation.
AI.motivation: Existing analog logical rotations in early fault-tolerant quantum algorithms have error scaling O(pφ), which is not fault-tolerant but works for sufficiently small φ. The authors aim to improve this error scaling without resorting to fallback synthesis.
AI.method: The paper introduces the "balanced fusion" technique, which improves error scaling through an improved analysis of the accumulation of coherent error terms in analog logical rotations.
AI.result: The balanced fusion technique achieves error scaling of O(p φ^{1.5}), compared to the previous O(pφ).
AI.conclusion: Balanced fusion improves the viability of analog logical rotations for small rotation angles as an alternative to cultivation-powered rotation synthesis.

title: Component-Level Inverse Design of Transmon Qubits Using Neural Networks
summary: Designing a superconducting qubit to realize specific Hamiltonian parameters typically requires iterating through a time and compute-intensive forward loop in which the designer chooses a layout geometry, simulates it, extracts circuit parameters such as capacitances, and refines the geometry. We study the inverse version of this task using a neural-network workflow that maps target Hamiltonian parameters directly to component-level layout parameters, which we subsequently demonstrate on a planar transmon layout. During training, we pair the inverse model with a frozen forward surrogate model and evaluate the loss in Hamiltonian space rather than in layout-parameter space. In validation against a conventional EM solver, 97% of generated designs produce usable geometries, and the inverse-plus-surrogate pipeline reaches mean percent errors of 0.73% for qubit frequency and 1.58% for anharmonicity, comparable to or below the fabrication and simulation-to-measurement uncertainty expected for academic-process transmon devices of this type. A single pipeline query takes approximately 56 ms on CPU, versus approximately 2 min for a conventional EM capacitance extraction on the same hardware, a speedup of more than 2,100 times. Batching minimizes the AI model inference overhead, reducing the runtime to 0.24 ms per sample on CPU and 2.5 microseconds per sample on GPU, resulting in speedups of 5.0 x 10^5 and 4.8 x 10^7, respectively, relative to a single conventional CPU EM extraction. Our results indicate that component-level inverse design usefully extends and complements conventional EM simulation, including for small datasets on the order of 1,000 samples.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a neural-network-based inverse design workflow for superconducting qubits that maps target Hamiltonian parameters directly to layout geometries, achieving 97% usable designs with sub-1% errors in qubit frequency and >2,100x speedup over conventional EM simulation on CPU, with even larger speedups via batching on GPU.
AI.motivation: Conventional superconducting qubit design requires iterative forward simulation loops (geometry → simulate → extract capacitances → refine), which is time- and compute-intensive. The authors aim to replace this with a direct inverse mapping from target Hamiltonian parameters to layout geometry.
AI.method: The authors develop an inverse neural network model paired with a frozen forward surrogate model. Training loss is computed in Hamiltonian parameter space rather than layout-parameter space. The approach is demonstrated on a planar transmon layout. Validation uses comparison against a conventional EM solver.
AI.result: 97% of generated designs produce usable geometries. Mean percent errors: 0.73% for qubit frequency, 1.58% for anharmonicity. Single pipeline query: ~56 ms on CPU vs ~2 min for conventional EM extraction (2,100x speedup). With batching: 0.24 ms/sample on CPU (5.0×10⁵ speedup), 2.5 μs/sample on GPU (4.8×10⁷ speedup).
AI.conclusion: Component-level inverse design usefully extends and complements conventional EM simulation, even for small datasets (~1,000 samples). The approach achieves accuracy comparable to or below fabrication and simulation-to-measurement uncertainty expected for academic-process transmon devices.

title: Hardness and Complexity Transition of Noisy Random Circuit Sampling
summary: Random circuit sampling (RCS) is a leading candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage, supported by strong complexity-theoretic evidence of hardness in the ideal setting and by rapid experimental progress to date. In practice, however, noise is unavoidable, and a central problem is to identify the noise-strength boundary between classically simulable and classically hard regimes. In this work, we establish an architecture-general hardness bound for this boundary for the standard local depolarizing noise of strength $γ$. Assuming the standard average-case #P-hardness conjecture for ideal RCS, we show that, for any circuit architecture satisfying this conjecture, noisy RCS on the same architecture remains hard to simulate classically within any inverse-polynomial total variation distance whenever $γ=O(\log n/(nd))$ for $n$-qubit circuits of depth $d$, unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. Crucially, noisy-RCS hardness follows without any additional conjectural or architecture-specific assumption beyond those already entering the ideal-RCS hardness framework. Our proof combines a low-degree polynomial extrapolation with a monotonicity reduction showing that efficient classical simulation at one depolarizing noise strength implies efficient simulation at every larger strength. Together, these ingredients transfer the standard ideal-RCS hardness conjecture to sampling hardness at a prespecified noise strength. Finally, combining the convergence-to-uniformity result of Dalzell et al. [Commun. Math. Phys. 405, 78 (2024)] with our monotonicity reduction yields efficient classical simulation for $γ=ω(\log n/(nd))$ on layered, regularly connected architectures. Thus, wherever the two architectural settings overlap, this identifies $γ=Θ(\log n/(nd))$ as the asymptotic complexity-transition scale.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a rigorous hardness boundary for noisy random circuit sampling (RCS) under local depolarizing noise. Assuming the standard #P-hardness conjecture for ideal RCS, noisy RCS remains classically hard when noise strength γ = O(log n/(nd)), and becomes efficiently simulable when γ = ω(log n/(nd)) on certain architectures, identifying a sharp complexity transition at γ = Θ(log n/(nd)).
AI.motivation: Noise is unavoidable in quantum computing experiments, and a central problem is to identify the noise-strength boundary between classically simulable and classically hard regimes for random circuit sampling, which is a leading candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage.
AI.method: The proof combines a low-degree polynomial extrapolation technique with a monotonicity reduction showing that efficient classical simulation at one depolarizing noise strength implies efficient simulation at every larger strength. This transfers the standard ideal-RCS hardness conjecture to sampling hardness at a prespecified noise strength.
AI.result: Noisy RCS remains hard to simulate classically within any inverse-polynomial total variation distance when γ = O(log n/(nd)), unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. On layered, regularly connected architectures, efficient classical simulation holds for γ = ω(log n/(nd)), identifying γ = Θ(log n/(nd)) as the asymptotic complexity-transition scale.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an architecture-general hardness bound for noisy RCS, showing that the transition between classical simulability and hardness occurs at noise strength γ = Θ(log n/(nd)), bridging the gap between theoretical complexity and experimental noise conditions.

title: An Operational Resolution of the Third-Particle Paradox
summary: We give an operational resolution of the third-particle paradox, relevant in the theory of quantum reference frames. The apparent paradox is that a system which is irrelevant in one quantum-reference-frame description can seem to become relevant after changing to another quantum reference frame, because the reduced state obtained after transforming a larger system need not agree with the state obtained by first discarding the extra system and then transforming. We argue that this comparison is not operationally meaningful unless the observables are transformed together with the states, or equivalently, unless the subsystem that needs to be discarded is properly identified. If the third particle is irrelevant for all measurements actually available in the original frame, then the transformed measurements form a restricted algebra in the new frame for which the third particle remains irrelevant. The paradox therefore results from replacing an operational statement about probabilities by a stronger, representation-dependent statement about equality of reduced density operators. We close by relating the question of when degrees of freedom may be discarded to the observable-induced, operational approach to subsystem structure.

AI.tldr: The third-particle paradox in quantum reference frames is resolved by showing it arises from comparing density operators rather than operational measurement probabilities; when observables are properly transformed alongside states, irrelevant particles remain irrelevant.
AI.motivation: To resolve the third-particle paradox in quantum reference frame theory, where a system irrelevant in one frame appears relevant after a frame change due to inconsistency between discarding-then-transforming versus transforming-then-discarding.
AI.method: Operational analysis showing the paradox stems from replacing probabilistic predictions with representation-dependent statements about reduced density operators; introducing observable-induced subsystem identification and transformed measurement algebras.
AI.result: When observables are transformed together with states, or when the correct subsystem is identified, the third particle remains irrelevant in the new frame, dissolving the paradox.
AI.conclusion: The paradox is not a genuine physical inconsistency but an artifact of comparing non-operational quantities; proper treatment requires transforming the full measurement algebra, and subsystem structure must be defined operationally via available observables.

title: Discrete-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution with uncertainty principle
summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution is a compelling framework for scalable quantum networks due to its seamless integration with existing optical communication infrastructure. However, a fundamental gap persists between theoretical protocols requiring ideal Gaussian modulation and the constrained, discrete-modulated signals dictated by practical high-speed hardware. Current security proofs for discrete modulation rely on semidefinite programming, which suffers from prohibitive computational overhead for high-order constellations and lacks direct physical insight into non-Gaussian modulation.In this Letter, we overcome this limitation by developing a security framework that obviates semidefinite programming in favor of an approach grounded fundamentally in the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. By introducing a multi-mode entanglement-source model to characterize non-Gaussian state preparation, we establish an explicit mapping between constellation geometry and the secret key rate. This framework effectively quantifies the security implications of hardware-limited, finite state preparation, enabling both numerical and analytical security analysis under high-order constellations. We experimentally validate our method on both discrete-component and integrated photonic platforms, demonstrating that a quadrature amplitude modulation format with 256 constellation points can asymptotically approach the Gaussian capacity limit. Beyond quantum key distribution, the principle of tightening uncertainty-constrained bounds via source-mode expansion offers a paradigm for exploring the information-theoretic properties of complex non-Gaussian systems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a security framework for continuous-variable quantum key distribution that replaces computationally expensive semidefinite programming with an approach based on the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, enabling efficient security analysis of high-order discrete modulation formats and experimentally demonstrating that 256-point QAM can approach the Gaussian capacity limit.
AI.motivation: A fundamental gap exists between theoretical CV-QKD protocols requiring ideal Gaussian modulation and the discrete-modulated signals dictated by practical high-speed hardware. Existing security proofs for discrete modulation rely on semidefinite programming, which suffers from prohibitive computational overhead for high-order constellations and lacks direct physical insight into non-Gaussian modulation.
AI.method: The authors develop a security framework that replaces semidefinite programming with an approach grounded in the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. They introduce a multi-mode entanglement-source model to characterize non-Gaussian state preparation, establishing an explicit mapping between constellation geometry and the secret key rate.
AI.result: The framework enables both numerical and analytical security analysis under high-order constellations. Experimental validation on discrete-component and integrated photonic platforms demonstrates that a QAM format with 256 constellation points can asymptotically approach the Gaussian capacity limit.
AI.conclusion: The principle of tightening uncertainty-constrained bounds via source-mode expansion offers a paradigm for exploring information-theoretic properties of complex non-Gaussian systems beyond quantum key distribution.

title: Heralded high-dimensional module-based quantum computation
summary: Parity measurements have been explored as building blocks for preparing and discriminating entangled states, as well as for implementing quantum computation. We first develop two alternative high-dimensional generalized parity modules, and then propose a procedure for constructing high-dimensional generalized module-based controlled-NOT gate. The construction of module-based quantum computing introduced here is deterministic, heralded, insensitive to the dimensionality of the computing basis, and postselection technique is not required. The result shows that out of $(d-1)!$ generalized parity modules, only modules $ \mathcal{P}=(j\ominus i)\bmod d$ and $ \mathcal{P}=(j \oplus i)\bmod d$ can be used as building blocks for high-dimensional quantum computing. Furthermore, we proposed an optical nondestructive scheme for implementing generalized parity module through quantum nondemolition measurements, and the success of the parity module is heralded by photon-number-resolving detectors and single-photon detectors.

AI.tldr: This paper develops high-dimensional generalized parity modules and a deterministic, heralded, postselection-free construction of module-based CNOT gates for quantum computing. It identifies only two specific parity modules out of (d-1)! as viable building blocks and proposes an optical nondestructive implementation using quantum nondemolition measurements.
AI.motivation: To develop high-dimensional generalized parity modules as building blocks for quantum computing and construct module-based CNOT gates that are deterministic, heralded, and insensitive to dimensionality without requiring postselection.
AI.method: Two high-dimensional generalized parity modules are developed, from which a procedure for constructing a module-based controlled-NOT gate is proposed. Optical nondestructive implementation via quantum nondemolition measurements is described, using photon-number-resolving and single-photon detectors for heralding.
AI.result: Out of (d-1)! generalized parity modules, only modules of the form P=(j⊖i) mod d and P=(j⊕i) mod d serve as suitable building blocks for high-dimensional quantum computing.
AI.conclusion: The proposed module-based quantum computing approach is deterministic, heralded, postselection-free, and scalable to arbitrary dimensions; the optical nondestructive scheme successfully implements the generalized parity module.

title: Multicritical dissipative phase transitions manipulated by dipole--dipole interactions
summary: Precise control of criticality in superradiant phase transitions is essential for quantum state engineering and the simulation of nonequilibrium phase transitions. Here, we investigate theoretically multicritical phenomena in a dissipative two-Rydberg-atom cavity--QED system. The intrinisic dipole--dipole interaction between the two Rydberg atoms restructures the energy-level landscape of the atomic subsystem, thereby significantly modifying the boundary of the continuous second-order superradiant phase transition, and shifting both the phase boundary and the multicritical point toward weaker atom--cavity strengths. For sufficiently strong dipole--dipole interactions, the continuous second-order phase transition and the multicritical point both disappear, leaving only a discontinuous first--order phase transition that enables the emergence of a superradiant phase even at arbitrarily weak atom--cavity coupling. This work is of fundamental interest for studying dissipative quantum phase transitions, with potential implications for quantum precision measurement and quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper studies multicritical phenomena in a dissipative two-Rydberg-atom cavity-QED system, showing that dipole-dipole interactions between Rydberg atoms shift phase boundaries and multicritical points toward weaker coupling, and can eliminate the continuous second-order transition and multicritical point entirely, leaving only a first-order transition that enables superradiance at arbitrarily weak coupling.
AI.motivation: Precise control of criticality in superradiant phase transitions is essential for quantum state engineering and simulating nonequilibrium phase transitions, motivating the study of multicritical phenomena in this system.
AI.method: The authors theoretically investigate a dissipative cavity-QED system with two Rydberg atoms, incorporating intrinsic dipole-dipole interactions that restructure the atomic energy-level landscape.
AI.result: Dipole-dipole interactions modify the boundary of the continuous second-order superradiant phase transition, shifting both the phase boundary and multicritical point toward weaker atom-cavity strengths. For sufficiently strong interactions, the second-order transition and multicritical point disappear, leaving only a first-order transition that allows superradiance at arbitrarily weak coupling.
AI.conclusion: The work is fundamentally interesting for studying dissipative quantum phase transitions and has potential implications for quantum precision measurement and quantum sensing.

title: Random unitary circuits with constant spectral gap
summary: We prove constant lower bounds for the spectral gap of the following random walks on unitary groups $\mathsf{SU}(2^n)$ on $n$ qubits. (i) Random Pauli Rotation: choose an $n$-qubit Pauli operator $P$ and an angle $θ\in \mathbb R / 2π\mathbb Z$, both uniformly at random, and apply $e^{\mathrm i θP}$. (ii) Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit: choose $n-1$ unitaries $U_{i}$ uniformly at random from $\mathsf{SU}(4)$ independently, and apply $U_{2j-1}$ on two qubits $2j-1, 2j$ and then $U_{2j}$ on two qubits $2j, 2j+1$. Importantly, the spectral gaps are independent of $n$ and apply for all finite dimensional unitary representations of $\mathsf{SU}(2^n)$ uniformly, including those that appear in unitary $t$-designs. We also prove analogous constant gap results for Clifford unitaries, which are indispensable for our result on Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit.

AI.tldr: This paper proves constant (n-independent) lower bounds on spectral gaps for two random walks on SU(2^n): Random Pauli Rotation and Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit, with results applying uniformly to all finite-dimensional unitary representations, including those in unitary t-designs. Analogous constant gap results for Clifford unitaries are also established.
AI.motivation: To establish dimension-independent convergence rates for random quantum processes on n qubits, which is crucial for understanding scrambling, thermalization, and the generation of unitary t-designs in many-body quantum systems.
AI.method: The paper analyzes two specific random walks: (i) Random Pauli Rotation—applying e^{iθP} with uniformly random Pauli P and angle θ; (ii) Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit—alternating layers of random SU(4) gates on a 1D qubit chain. The analysis leverages representation theory and proves constant spectral gaps independent of n for all finite-dimensional unitary representations, with Clifford unitaries playing a key role in the brickwork circuit proof.
AI.result: The spectral gaps for both random walks are constant (independent of n), and the results hold uniformly across all finite-dimensional unitary representations of SU(2^n). Additionally, constant gap results for random walks on Clifford unitaries are proven, which are essential for the brickwork circuit analysis.
AI.conclusion: Random Pauli rotations and brickwork random unitary circuits achieve rapid mixing with a rate that does not degrade with system size, offering strong guarantees for quantum information processing tasks such as efficient generation of unitary t-designs and quantum chaos.

title: Generation of bright quantum high-order harmonic driven by combined coherent and bright squeezed vacuum light
summary: Attosecond quantum light, formed by the superposition of high-order harmonics driven by intense quantum light, opens new routes to probe quantum-mechanical correlations in matter. In this study, we have investigated the macroscopic propagation effects of quantum high-order harmonics generated by the combination of strong coherent and weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) lasers interacting with atomic gas. Our results reveal that the pressure-dependent intensity of harmonics arising from absorbing or emitting BSV photons differs from that of harmonics generated using only strong coherent pulses. Macroscopic propagation simulations indicate that the action phase of harmonics is perturbed by the weak BSV pulses. This perturbation modulates the phase mismatch of sub-cycle attosecond bursts and affects their quantum properties when the gas pressure varies. The ability to generate bright quantum high-order harmonics lays a foundation for the establishment and application of attosecond quantum spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: This study investigates macroscopic propagation effects of quantum high-order harmonics generated by combining strong coherent and weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) lasers in atomic gas, showing that BSV pulses perturb the action phase and phase mismatch of attosecond bursts, affecting their quantum properties with pressure variation, and laying groundwork for attosecond quantum spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: To explore macroscopic propagation effects of quantum high-order harmonics generated by strong coherent and weak bright squeezed vacuum lasers, aiming to understand phase mismatch modulation and quantum property changes under varying gas pressure for advancing attosecond quantum spectroscopy.
AI.method: The study uses macroscopic propagation simulations of quantum high-order harmonics generated by combining strong coherent laser pulses with weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) pulses interacting with atomic gas, analyzing pressure-dependent harmonic intensity and phase mismatch.
AI.result: Pressure-dependent harmonic intensity differs between harmonics from absorbing/emitting BSV photons and those from coherent pulses alone. BSV pulses perturb the action phase, modulating phase mismatch of sub-cycle attosecond bursts and their quantum properties with gas pressure variation.
AI.conclusion: Generating bright quantum high-order harmonics forms a foundation for establishing and applying attosecond quantum spectroscopy.

title: An Analytically Trained Variational Surrogate for Quantum Phase Estimation on NISQ Hardware
summary: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is a foundational algorithm for molecular ground-state energy estimation, but its deep circuit requirements make direct hardware execution impractical on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. We present an analytically grounded variational surrogate framework in which a shallow Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) is trained to reproduce the QPE measurement distribution without any quantum circuit simulation. The training target is computed entirely classically via the Dirichlet kernel, evaluated directly from the Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) ground-state energy, the ancilla qubit count, and the time evolution parameter, eliminating the exponentially scaling simulation bottleneck of prior surrogate approaches. We apply this framework to the hydrogen molecule (H$_2$) with a symmetry-tapered Hamiltonian, conducting a four-stage experimental investigation on IBM Quantum hardware. Stage 1 compares linear and full entangler topologies for the $R_Y$-$R_Z$-$CZ$ ansatz, with and without XpXm Dynamical Decoupling (DD), across four distributional metrics (Hellinger distance, fidelity error, total variation distance, Jensen-Shannon divergence), identifying the linear entangler as optimal. Stage 2 varies VQC layers ($p=1$ to $5$) for the linear-entangler ansatz, identifying single-layer depth as optimal under hardware noise. Stage 3 applies this configuration to the reduced $R_Y$-$CZ$ ansatz, comparing ideal and noisy simulator-trained parameters. A supplementary noise analysis at $p \in \{8,64\}$ characterizes the depth-dependent interplay between circuit depth and DD effectiveness. The framework enables faithful QPE mimicry using a linearly scaling VQC, recovering the ground-state energy within the chemical accuracy threshold (1 kcal/mol), constituting a scalable, hardware-efficient paradigm for QPE-based molecular energy estimation on NISQ devices.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a variational surrogate framework where a shallow Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) is trained classically (via Dirichlet kernel) to reproduce the Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) measurement distribution, eliminating exponential simulation costs. Applied to H₂ on IBM hardware, it identifies optimal topologies (linear entangler), layer depth (single-layer), and ansatz configurations, recovering ground-state energy within chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol) using a linearly scaling VQC.
AI.motivation: Quantum Phase Estimation is foundational for molecular ground-state energy estimation but requires deep circuits impractical on NISQ devices. Prior surrogate approaches suffered from exponentially scaling simulation bottlenecks, motivating a more efficient, hardware-compatible framework.
AI.method: A variational surrogate framework trains a shallow VQC to mimic QPE measurement distributions. The training target is computed classically via the Dirichlet kernel from the FCI ground-state energy, ancilla count, and time evolution parameter—no quantum circuit simulation needed. A four-stage experimental study on IBM Quantum hardware evaluates entangler topologies, layer depths, ansatz variations, and dynamical decoupling for H₂ with a symmetry-tapered Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The linear entangler topology and single-layer depth were identified as optimal under hardware noise. The framework recovers the ground-state energy within chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol) using a linearly scaling VQC, with a supplementary noise analysis at depths p∈{8,64} characterizing depth-DD interplay.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework constitutes a scalable, hardware-efficient paradigm for QPE-based molecular energy estimation on NISQ devices, eliminating exponential simulation costs while maintaining faithfulness to QPE distributions and chemical accuracy.

title: Large deviations in quantum dynamics and complexity
summary: We study three definitions of large deviation in many-body quantum dynamics: (i) via the full distribution of an extensive observable, (ii) via the distribution of measurement outcomes (from a continuous monitoring of the observable) over a time interval $t \le t_{\max}$, and (iii) via the distribution of expectation values over $t \le t_{\max}$. In generic systems without conservation laws, the large deviation function (i) reaches its longtime limit at $t \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$, independently of system size $N$. (ii) and (iii) reach their longtime limit at $t \sim e^{ N}$ and $t \sim \exp(e^{N})$, respectively. Before that, there is a {\it sharp} frontier between the explored and unexplored outcomes/expectation values; their distribution equals the longtime limit truncated at values that drift with $t_{\max}$. We propose that the evolution of these values with $t_{\max}$ provides a measure of quantum complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper studies three definitions of large deviation in many-body quantum dynamics, finding that the large deviation function (i) reaches its longtime limit at O(1) time, while (ii) and (iii) reach it at exponentially long times (e^N and exp(e^N) respectively), with a sharp frontier between explored and unexplored outcomes that drifts with time, proposed as a measure of quantum complexity.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize the timescales and behavior of large deviation functions in many-body quantum dynamics, particularly for systems without conservation laws, and to connect these to quantum complexity.
AI.method: The authors study three definitions of large deviation: (i) full distribution of an extensive observable, (ii) distribution of measurement outcomes from continuous monitoring over time, and (iii) distribution of expectation values over time. They analyze the timescales for reaching the longtime limit for each definition and examine the frontier between explored and unexplored regions.
AI.result: (i) reaches longtime limit at t~O(1) independent of system size N; (ii) reaches longtime limit at t~e^N; (iii) reaches longtime limit at t~exp(e^N). Before reaching the limit, there is a sharp frontier between explored and unexplored outcomes/expectation values, with the distribution equaling the longtime limit truncated at values that drift with t_max.
AI.conclusion: The evolution of the drifting frontier values with t_max provides a measure of quantum complexity, suggesting that different definitions of large deviation probe vastly different timescales and reveal different aspects of quantum many-body dynamics.

title: Compact deterministic liquid-crystal polarization controller with single-measurement direct control
summary: Polarization controllers (PCs) and their control algorithms are critical for compensating environmental disturbances and maintaining signal fidelity in polarization-sensitive photonic systems. However, existing controllers often involve trade-offs among key performance metrics, while associated control algorithms either converge inefficiently or require multiple state-of-polarization (SOP) measurements. This work presents a compact deterministic liquid-crystal polarization controller (LC-PC) with balanced overall performance, featuring low insertion loss (<1 dB), low driving voltage (<6 V), and full Poincaré sphere coverage. The device exhibits highly predictable and repeatable polarization modulation characterized by SOP-independent trajectory normal vectors, enabling a single-measurement direct-calculation algorithm with an angular error below 2°. The combination of this compact deterministic LC-PC and its efficient control scheme provides a practical solution for polarization management in quantum key distribution, optical sensing, and advanced photonic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a compact liquid-crystal polarization controller (LC-PC) with low loss, low voltage, and full Poincaré sphere coverage, using a novel single-measurement direct-calculation algorithm with <2° angular error for efficient polarization management.
AI.motivation: Existing polarization controllers involve trade-offs among key performance metrics, and their control algorithms either converge inefficiently or require multiple SOP measurements.
AI.method: A compact deterministic LC-PC with SOP-independent trajectory normal vectors, enabling a single-measurement direct-calculation control algorithm.
AI.result: Low insertion loss (<1 dB), low driving voltage (<6 V), full Poincaré sphere coverage, and angular error below 2° using the single-measurement algorithm.
AI.conclusion: The combination of this LC-PC and its efficient control scheme provides a practical solution for polarization management in quantum key distribution, optical sensing, and advanced photonic systems.

title: A Quantum Interface Between Neutral-Atoms and Trapped-Ions Quantum Registers
summary: Hybrid quantum systems combining neutral atoms and trapped ions offer the prospect of integrating the scalability of atom arrays with the high-fidelity control available in trapped-ion platforms. Here we propose and analyze a quantum interface between individually trapped neutral atoms and a trapped-ion crystal. In our scheme, a neutral 88Sr atom trapped in optical tweezers interacts with a small 88Sr+ ion crystal, and by exciting the atom to a Rydberg state, the atom-ion polarization interaction is strongly enhanced, resulting in a state-dependent modification of the ions' collective motional modes. We show that this shift enables conditional control of a MS gate, allowing the neutral atom to act as a control qubit for an entangling operation between two ions. We investigate the feasibility of the scheme by analyzing Rydberg trapping in the combined optical tweezers and Paul trap potentials, identifying negative-polarizability Rydberg states as particularly favorable for stable confinement. We further evaluate the relevant trapping conditions, Rydberg lifetimes, and coherence requirements, and show that the proposed interface is compatible with realistic experimental parameters. These results establish a practical route toward deterministic atom-ion hybrid quantum gates and quantum interfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and analyzes a hybrid quantum interface between neutral 88Sr atoms trapped in optical tweezers and a trapped 88Sr+ ion crystal. By exciting the neutral atom to a Rydberg state, the atom-ion polarization interaction is enhanced, enabling state-dependent shifts in the ions' collective motional modes. This allows the neutral atom to act as a control qubit for an entangling MS gate between two ions. The scheme is shown to be feasible with realistic experimental parameters.
AI.motivation: To integrate the scalability of neutral atom arrays with the high-fidelity control of trapped-ion platforms by proposing a practical quantum interface between these two modalities.
AI.method: The scheme uses a 88Sr atom in optical tweezers interacting with a 88Sr+ ion crystal. The atom is excited to a Rydberg state to strongly enhance the atom-ion polarization interaction, causing a state-dependent shift in the ions' collective motional modes. This shift enables conditional control of an MS gate. The feasibility is analyzed by studying Rydberg trapping in combined optical tweezers and Paul trap potentials, identifying negative-polarizability Rydberg states for stable confinement.
AI.result: The proposed interface is compatible with realistic experimental parameters, including appropriate trapping conditions, Rydberg lifetimes, and coherence requirements. Negative-polarizability Rydberg states are identified as suitable for stable confinement in the combined potential.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a practical route toward deterministic atom-ion hybrid quantum gates and quantum interfaces, merging the advantages of neutral atom scalability and trapped-ion control.

title: On-chip Radio Frequency Maser
summary: Room-temperature solid-state masers offer exceptional frequency selectivity and ultra-low noise for weak-signal detection. However, their reliance on bulky metallic resonators has significantly hindered integration, miniaturization, and extension to lower frequencies. Here, we demonstrate the first on-chip radio-frequency maser operating at room temperature, exploiting optically pumped triplet states of pentacene. The device produces stimulated emission at 106.62 MHz and enables ultra-sensitive microwave magnetic-field detection with a sensitivity of ($\sim 10\,\rm{fT/\sqrt{Hz}}$), functioning simultaneously as a local oscillator and a sensor. By actively controlling microwave dissipation, we achieve efficient regulation of the maser output, revealing a key mechanism for tuning emission in open cavity-free systems. This work extends pentacene-based masers into the radio-frequency regime and establishes a highly integrated on-chip architecture for room-temperature masers, offering a new pathway toward portable quantum devices.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the first on-chip room-temperature radio-frequency maser using optically pumped pentacene triplet states, achieving 106.62 MHz stimulated emission and fT-level magnetic-field sensitivity in an integrated cavity-free architecture.
AI.motivation: Room-temperature solid-state masers have relied on bulky metallic resonators, hindering integration, miniaturization, and extension to lower frequencies.
AI.method: An on-chip architecture using optically pumped triplet states of pentacene, with active control of microwave dissipation to regulate maser output in an open cavity-free system.
AI.result: Achieved stimulated emission at 106.62 MHz and ultra-sensitive microwave magnetic-field detection with sensitivity ~10 fT/√Hz, functioning as both local oscillator and sensor.
AI.conclusion: Extends pentacene-based masers to the radio-frequency regime, establishes a highly integrated on-chip architecture for room-temperature masers, and offers a pathway toward portable quantum devices.

title: Vacuum-induced interference in light scattering by multilevel atomic chains
summary: We investigate cooperative light scattering by an ordered chain of multilevel atoms, which possess two quasi-resonant transitions with parallel dipole moments. Interference between dipole transitions induced by coupling with the vacuum gives rise to so called cross-damping and cross-shifts, that modify the incoherent and coherent dynamics and can be manifest in the spectroscopic properties of the emitted light. We determine the excitation spectrum when the atomic chain is driven by an external laser in the limit in which the dipolar transitions can be described by harmonic oscillators and the scattering is coherent. We show that the interplay of multilevel interference and superradiance can give rise to measurable effects in chains of alkali-metal atoms.

AI.tldr: The paper studies cooperative light scattering in ordered chains of multilevel atoms with parallel dipole transitions, showing that interference between dipole transitions via vacuum coupling leads to cross-damping and cross-shifts, and that multilevel interference combined with superradiance produces measurable effects in alkali-metal atom chains under coherent driving.
AI.motivation: To understand how multilevel interference and cross-coupling effects (cross-damping and cross-shifts) modify cooperative light scattering in ordered atomic chains, going beyond the usual two-level atom approximation.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using harmonic oscillator models for dipolar transitions in ordered chains of multilevel atoms with parallel dipole moments, driven by an external laser in the coherent scattering limit.
AI.result: Interference between dipole transitions via vacuum coupling induces cross-damping and cross-shifts that alter both incoherent and coherent dynamics; these effects are measurable in the excitation spectrum of alkali-metal atom chains.
AI.conclusion: The interplay of multilevel interference and superradiance yields observable spectroscopic signatures in alkali-metal atomic chains, highlighting the importance of multilevel effects in cooperative scattering.

title: Picosecond-resolved entanglement distribution over an urban free-space channel
summary: Time-evolving entangled states describe quantum particles whose correlations evolve in time according to a well-defined dynamics. Such states can be generated in a variety of physical systems and are promising resources for several quantum technologies, ranging from quantum clock synchronization to quantum communication. However, their full potential is currently limited by the fact that the entanglement dynamics often occur on timescales comparable to the achievable synchronization precision, especially in experiments aimed at distributing entanglement through noisy urban channels. In this context, accurate timing is not merely a technical detail, but a fundamental requirement for faithfully observing and exploiting the underlying quantum correlations. Here, we demonstrate the faithful distribution of a fast-evolving entangled state over a 270 m free-space channel connecting two buildings in the center of Rome. The developed system incorporates a synchronization device capable of achieving sub-50 ps timing accuracy between the two ends of the link while simultaneously supporting channel stabilization. Our results demonstrate that time-evolving entanglement can be reliably transmitted through a noisy urban free-space channel, representing an important benchmark toward long-distance free-space quantum communication and the future implementation of time-correlated entangled states in demanding scenarios such as satellite-based quantum networks.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the faithful distribution of fast-evolving entangled states over a 270 m urban free-space channel with sub-50 ps synchronization accuracy, enabling reliable quantum communication in noisy environments.
AI.motivation: Time-evolving entangled states are promising for quantum technologies but limited by entanglement dynamics occurring on timescales comparable to synchronization precision, especially in noisy urban channels. Accurate timing is a fundamental requirement for faithfully observing quantum correlations.
AI.method: A system incorporating a synchronization device achieving sub-50 ps timing accuracy over a 270 m free-space channel connecting two buildings in Rome, while simultaneously supporting channel stabilization.
AI.result: Successful faithful distribution of fast-evolving entangled states through a noisy urban free-space channel over 270 m with sub-50 ps timing accuracy.
AI.conclusion: This work represents an important benchmark toward long-distance free-space quantum communication and future implementation of time-correlated entangled states in demanding scenarios such as satellite-based quantum networks.

title: Conditional probabilities in quantum-optical settings
summary: We examine conditional probabilities derived from the joint noisy measurement of two complementary observables. We show that conditioning on one variable can lead to reduction of uncertainty in the other one, even completely eliminating uncertainty. We show that the conditional distribution cannot, in general, be represented in Born form using the marginal positive operator valued measure and any physical system state, nor can it be derived from typical rules of state reduction. We examine these issues in two basic quantum-optical schemes. These are double homodyne detection and a qubit measurement.

AI.tldr: Conditional probabilities from joint noisy measurement of complementary observables can reduce uncertainty in the other variable, but cannot generally be represented in Born form using marginal POVM and any physical state, nor derived from standard state reduction rules. This is examined in double homodyne detection and qubit measurement.
AI.motivation: To investigate how conditioning on one variable from joint noisy measurements of complementary observables affects uncertainty in the other variable, and to examine whether such conditional probabilities can be described by standard quantum mechanical rules like the Born rule or state reduction.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of conditional probabilities from joint noisy measurements of complementary observables, examined through two quantum-optical schemes: double homodyne detection and qubit measurement.
AI.result: Conditioning on one variable can reduce or even eliminate uncertainty in the complementary variable. However, the resulting conditional distribution cannot generally be expressed in Born form using the marginal POVM and any physical system state, nor can it be derived from typical state reduction rules.
AI.conclusion: Standard quantum mechanical formalisms (Born rule with marginal POVM, state reduction rules) are insufficient to describe conditional probabilities arising from joint noisy measurements of complementary observables.

title: Entanglement, Evolutionary Stability, and Strategy-Space Dependence in an EWL Quantum Game
summary: We examine how Eisert--Wilkens--Lewenstein (EWL) quantization affects evolutionary stability in a symmetric $2\times2$ game whose interior mixed Nash equilibrium is not evolutionarily stable. In the restricted two-parameter EWL strategy space, the quantum equilibrium $s^*=(π/2,π/4)$ becomes a strict symmetric Nash equilibrium, and hence an evolutionarily stable strategy, for every $γ>0$. Extending the admissible pure strategies to the full three-parameter $SU(2)$ family preserves the Nash equilibrium but introduces a continuum of payoff-neutral mutants, causing strictness and the second ESS condition to fail. Thus, entanglement stabilizes the equilibrium only within the restricted EWL strategy space; the effect does not survive enlargement to full $SU(2)$.

AI.tldr: EWL quantization stabilizes the interior mixed Nash equilibrium in a symmetric 2x2 game by making it a strict symmetric Nash equilibrium (and thus an ESS) in the restricted two-parameter strategy space, but this stabilizing effect vanishes when extending to full SU(2) due to the emergence of payoff-neutral mutants.
